decks.title: Fertilisation, Seed and Fruit — Part 1: Double fertilisation and post-fertilisation events
goals: Explain double fertilisation and triple fusion and their significance
Distinguish cellular, nuclear and helobial endosperm and define perisperm
Describe embryo development in dicots and monocots

slides.heading: Fertilisation, Seed and Fruit
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what happens after the pollen tube reaches the embryo sac.

nodes.label: Ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit

visual.alt: Flow from pollen tube entry to seed and fruit

slides.narration: Fertilisation is followed by a remarkable set of changes. The zygote grows into an embryo, a food tissue forms around it, the ovule matures into a seed, and the ovary ripens into a fruit. Together these are called post-fertilisation events.

slides.heading: Double fertilisation
slides.body_md: The pollen tube releases **two male gametes** into a synergid. One fuses with the **egg** (**syngamy**) to form the **diploid zygote**. The other fuses with the **two polar nuclei** (**triple fusion**) to form the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**. Two fusions in one embryo sac make **double fertilisation**, unique to flowering plants.

slides.narration: Because two separate fusion events happen in the same embryo sac, the process is called double fertilisation. The central cell, now holding the primary endosperm nucleus, becomes the primary endosperm cell, which grows into the endosperm. The zygote grows into the embryo.

slides.heading: Significance of double fertilisation
slides.body_md: Double fertilisation links the formation of food tissue to successful fertilisation.

rows: Restores the diploid number in the zygote; combines characters of two parents
Forms the triploid endosperm, a nutritive tissue for the developing embryo
Food tissue is made only when an egg is fertilised, so the plant does not waste food on ovules that fail

visual.alt: Table of the significance of syngamy and triple fusion

slides.narration: Endosperm forms only when fertilisation has happened. The plant therefore invests food reserves only in ovules that will become seeds, an efficient strategy found in flowering plants.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ploidy in the seed
slides.body_md: A plant has 2n = 14. Give the number of chromosomes in the zygote, the primary endosperm nucleus, the perisperm and the seed coat.
bullets: Zygote: $n + n = 7 + 7 = 14$.
Primary endosperm nucleus: $n + n + n = 21$.
Perisperm (persistent nucellus) and seed coat (integuments) are maternal tissues: $2n = 14$.

visual.alt: Worked table: zygote 14, endosperm 21, perisperm and seed coat 14

slides.narration: Ask where each tissue comes from. The zygote joins two haploid nuclei, so it has fourteen chromosomes. The endosperm joins three, so it has twenty-one. The perisperm and seed coat are just maternal tissue, so they keep the diploid number, fourteen.

slides.body_md: Which nuclei take part in triple fusion?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the nuclei that meet the second male gamete.

slides.heading: Endosperm: three types
slides.body_md: Endosperm development **precedes** embryo development. The primary endosperm cell divides repeatedly to form a **triploid endosperm** storing food.

rows: PEN divides repeatedly by free-nuclear division; walls may form later from the periphery
Coconut: the water is free-nuclear endosperm, the white kernel is cellular
Every division of the PEN is followed by wall formation
First division forms two unequal cells; the larger divides free-nuclearly, the smaller cellularly or not at all

visual.alt: Table of nuclear, cellular and helobial endosperm with examples

slides.narration: Nuclear endosperm is the commonest type. Tender coconut water is a free-nuclear endosperm made up of thousands of nuclei, and the surrounding white kernel is the cellular part. The endosperm may be used up before the seed matures, as in pea and bean, or may persist, as in cereals and castor.

slides.heading: Perisperm and seed coverings
slides.body_md: In some seeds, remnants of the **nucellus** persist. This **residual, persistent nucellus** is the **perisperm**, e.g. **black pepper** and **beet**. It is **diploid** and maternal, unlike the triploid endosperm.

rows: Primary endosperm cell after triple fusion

visual.alt: Table comparing endosperm, perisperm, seed coat and pericarp

slides.narration: Not every food tissue in a seed is endosperm. In black pepper and beet, part of the nucellus survives as perisperm. Remember that the perisperm, the seed coat and the fruit wall are all maternal and diploid.

slides.heading: Embryo development in dicots
slides.body_md: The embryo develops at the **micropylar end** of the embryo sac. The zygote divides to form the **proembryo**, then **globular**, **heart-shaped** and mature stages. A dicot embryo has an **embryonal axis** with **two cotyledons**: above them the **epicotyl** ends in the **plumule**; below, the **hypocotyl** ends in the **radicle** with a **root cap**.

slides.heading: Embryo development in monocots

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting for a pod
slides.body_md: A pea pod contains 40 seeds. What is the minimum number of ovules, pollen grains, male gametes and meiotic divisions needed? (Each embryo sac is monosporic; each pollen mother cell gives 4 pollen grains.)
bullets: Ovules $=$ seeds $= 40$; pollen grains $= 40$ (one tube per ovule); male gametes $= 2 \times 40 = 80$.
Female meioses $= 40$ (one MMC per ovule); male meioses $= \dfrac{40}{4} = 10$.
Total meioses $= 40 + 10 = 50$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 50 meioses for 40 seeds

slides.narration: Each seed needs one ovule and one pollen grain, and each pollen grain supplies two male gametes. One meiosis makes one embryo sac, but one meiosis on the male side makes four pollen grains. So forty seeds need forty plus ten, fifty meioses.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Double fertilisation: syngamy (egg + male gamete → 2n zygote) and triple fusion (2 polar nuclei + male gamete → 3n PEN).
Endosperm forms before the embryo: nuclear (coconut water), cellular (Petunia, Datura), helobial (many monocots).
Perisperm: persistent nucellus (black pepper, beet), 2n.
Dicot embryo: proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature; two cotyledons, plumule, radicle.
Monocot embryo: scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza.

visual.alt: Summary table of ploidy of three products

slides.narration: To recap: two male gametes give two fusions, a diploid zygote and a triploid endosperm. Endosperm forms first, in nuclear, cellular or helobial fashion. Then the embryo develops, with two cotyledons in dicots and a scutellum in grasses.

bullets: Define **double fertilisation** and **triple fusion** separately; give the **ploidy** of each product.

slides.narration: Exam tips. Define both fusions and give the ploidy of each product. Learn an example for each endosperm type. Separate endosperm from perisperm. And practise both embryo diagrams.

slides.heading: Seeds and fruits
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the products of fertilisation, and the exceptions to the usual route.

visual.alt: Flow showing ovule becoming seed and ovary becoming fruit

slides.narration: The seed is the final product of sexual reproduction in angiosperms, often described as the fertilised ovule. The ovary wall becomes the fruit wall, or pericarp, and protects and helps disperse the seeds.

slides.heading: A dicot seed: bean
slides.body_md: A bean seed has a **seed coat** of two layers, the outer **testa** and inner **tegmen**. The **hilum** is the scar where the seed was attached to its stalk; the **micropyle** lies beside it. The embryo has two large **cotyledons** storing food and an embryonal axis with **plumule** and **radicle**. The endosperm is used up: the seed is **non-albuminous (exalbuminous)**.

slides.heading: A monocot grain: maize
slides.body_md: In a maize grain the **pericarp is fused with the seed coat**. Below it lies the **aleurone layer**, a protein-rich layer around the starchy **endosperm**. The embryo has a **scutellum**, a **coleoptile** over the plumule and a **coleorhiza** over the radicle. The endosperm persists: the seed is **albuminous**.

slides.heading: Albuminous and non-albuminous seeds
slides.body_md: Seeds differ in whether the endosperm survives to maturity.

rows: Used up during development; food stored in cotyledons

visual.alt: Table comparing albuminous and non-albuminous seeds

slides.narration: Cereals and castor keep their endosperm, so their seeds are albuminous. Pea, bean and groundnut use it up, so their seeds are non-albuminous. As seeds mature, their water content falls to about ten to fifteen percent and many enter dormancy.

bullets: Castor: endosperm present → **albuminous**; food in **endosperm**.
Groundnut: two thick cotyledons, no endosperm → **non-albuminous**; food in **cotyledons**.
Wheat grain: large starchy endosperm under the aleurone layer → **albuminous**.
Black pepper: food in persistent nucellus → stored in the **perisperm**.

slides.narration: Look for where the food is stored. If it is in a separate tissue around the embryo, the seed is albuminous, unless that tissue is the nucellus, which is perisperm. If the cotyledons are fat and fleshy and there is no other tissue, the seed is non-albuminous.

slides.heading: True and false fruits
slides.body_md: A **true fruit** develops only from the **ovary**. In a **false fruit**, other floral parts also contribute — most often the **thalamus**. Fruits formed without fertilisation are **parthenocarpic**.

visual.alt: Table of true, false and parthenocarpic fruits with examples

slides.narration: In most plants, by the time the fruit develops from the ovary the other floral parts have withered. In apple and strawberry, however, the fleshy part you eat is mostly the thalamus, so these are false fruits.

bullets: Mango → **mesocarp** (part of the pericarp, from the ovary wall).
Coconut → **endosperm**, both solid (kernel) and liquid (water).
Apple → mainly the **thalamus**, so apple is a false fruit.
Wheat → **endosperm** of the grain.

slides.narration: Trace each edible part to its origin. The flesh of a mango is fruit wall. Coconut and wheat give us endosperm from triple fusion. And the crisp flesh of an apple is mostly swollen thalamus.

slides.heading: Significance of seeds, fruits and dispersal
slides.body_md: Seeds and fruits gave angiosperms great advantages.

rows: Do not depend on water for pollination and fertilisation; carry food reserves; can stay dormant and viable for long (a lupine seed about 10,000 years old germinated; a date palm seed about 2,000 years old was viable)
Products of sexual reproduction generate new genetic combinations
Colonises new habitats and reduces crowding and competition near the parent

visual.alt: Table of the significance of seeds, fruits and dispersal

slides.narration: Seeds are the basis of agriculture: their dormancy and long life let us store them as food and planting material. Fruits protect the seeds and help disperse them by wind, water or animals to new places.

slides.heading: Apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy
slides.body_md: Some plants form seeds or fruits outside the usual route.

rows: Seeds form without fertilisation (asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction), e.g. from a diploid egg or from nucellar cells
Some Asteraceae and grasses; hybrid seed made apomictic would not segregate, so farmers could reuse it
More than one embryo in a seed, often from nucellar cells that grow into the embryo sac
Banana; can be induced by growth hormones

visual.alt: Table of apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy with examples

slides.narration: Apomixis gives seeds that are genetically identical to the parent. That is why breeders are interested in it: hybrid varieties lose their combination of characters when farmers sow their own seed, but apomictic hybrids would breed true year after year.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Bean: testa, tegmen, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons, plumule, radicle; non-albuminous.
Maize: pericarp fused with seed coat, aleurone layer, endosperm, scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza; albuminous.
True fruit from ovary only; false fruit with thalamus (apple, strawberry, cashew); parthenocarpic (banana).
Mango: epicarp, fleshy mesocarp, stony endocarp; coconut: fibrous mesocarp, shell, solid and liquid endosperm.
Apomixis (Asteraceae, grasses), polyembryony (citrus, mango), parthenocarpy (banana).

visual.alt: Summary table of edible parts

slides.narration: To recap: seeds may keep or use up their endosperm. Fruits may come from the ovary alone or include the thalamus. Mango and coconut are both drupes with different edible parts. And apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy bypass the usual route.

notes.title: Fertilisation, Seed and Fruit in Flowering Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Double fertilisation
sections.body_md:
**Events leading to fertilisation.** Compatible pollen germinates on the stigma; the pollen tube grows through the style, enters the ovule through the **micropyle**, and enters one of the **synergids**, guided by the **filiform apparatus**. It releases **two male gametes** into the cytoplasm of the synergid.

**Syngamy.** One male gamete fuses with the nucleus of the **egg cell** to form the **diploid zygote (2n)**.

**Triple fusion.** The other male gamete fuses with the **two polar nuclei** in the central cell to form the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN, 3n)**. Three haploid nuclei fuse, hence the name. The central cell becomes the **primary endosperm cell (PEC)**, which develops into the **endosperm**; the zygote develops into the **embryo**.

**Double fertilisation** — two fusion events (syngamy and triple fusion) in one embryo sac — is a characteristic feature of **angiosperms**.

**Significance:**
- Syngamy restores the **diploid** number and combines characters of **two parents**, giving variation.
- Triple fusion produces the **triploid endosperm**, a nutritive tissue for the embryo.
- Food tissue forms **only if fertilisation occurs**, so reserves are not wasted on unfertilised ovules.
- After fertilisation the **synergids and antipodals degenerate**.

sections.heading: 2. Post-fertilisation events: endosperm, perisperm and embryo
sections.body_md:
**Endosperm.** Endosperm development **precedes** embryo development. The PEC divides repeatedly to form a **triploid** endosperm tissue filled with reserve food, used to nourish the embryo.
- **Nuclear endosperm** (commonest): the PEN undergoes successive **free-nuclear** divisions; cell walls may later form from the periphery towards the centre. **Coconut**: tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm (thousands of nuclei) and the surrounding white kernel is cellular endosperm.
- **Cellular endosperm**: every nuclear division is followed by **wall formation** (e.g. **Petunia, Datura**).
- **Helobial endosperm**: the first division forms two **unequal** cells; the larger (micropylar) chamber develops free-nuclearly and the smaller (chalazal) one cellularly or not at all; common in **monocots** (e.g. Asphodelus).
- The endosperm may be **completely consumed** by the developing embryo (pea, groundnut, beans) or **persist** in the mature seed (castor, coconut, cereals).

**Perisperm.** In some seeds, remnants of the **nucellus** persist as a **residual, persistent nucellus** called **perisperm** (e.g. **black pepper, beet**). It is **diploid** and maternal.

**Embryo (embryogeny).** The embryo develops at the **micropylar end**. Most zygotes divide only after a certain amount of endosperm has formed — an adaptation that provides assured nutrition.
- **Dicot:** zygote → **proembryo** → **globular** → **heart-shaped** → mature embryo. The mature embryo has an **embryonal axis** and **two cotyledons**. The part above the cotyledons is the **epicotyl**, ending in the **plumule** (stem tip); the part below is the **hypocotyl**, ending in the **radicle** (root tip) covered by a **root cap**.
- **Monocot (grass):** only **one cotyledon**, the **scutellum**, situated towards one side (lateral) of the embryonal axis. At its lower end the axis has the radicle and root cap enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath, the **coleorhiza**. The shoot apex and a few leaf primordia are enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the **coleoptile**. An **epiblast** (a remnant of a second cotyledon) is present in some grasses.

sections.heading: 3. Seeds
sections.body_md:
In angiosperms the **seed** is the final product of sexual reproduction, often described as the **fertilised ovule**. Seeds form inside fruits. A seed typically consists of **seed coat(s)**, **cotyledon(s)** and an **embryonal axis**.

**Dicot seed — bean.** The **seed coat** has two layers, outer **testa** and inner **tegmen**. The **hilum** is a scar where the seed was attached to the fruit (funicle); the **micropyle** is a small pore above it. The embryo has two large, fleshy **cotyledons** and an embryonal axis with **plumule** and **radicle**. No endosperm remains.

**Monocot seed — maize grain.** The seed coat is membranous and generally **fused with the fruit wall (pericarp)**. The bulky **endosperm** stores food and is separated from the embryo by an epithelial layer; its outer protein-rich layer is the **aleurone layer**. The embryo is small, in a groove at one end, with one large shield-shaped cotyledon, the **scutellum**, and a short axis with **plumule** enclosed in the **coleoptile** and **radicle** enclosed in the **coleorhiza**.

**Albuminous (endospermic) seeds** retain part of the endosperm (wheat, maize, barley, castor, coconut). **Non-albuminous (exalbuminous) seeds** have no residual endosperm, as it is consumed during embryo development (pea, groundnut, bean, gram).

As seeds mature, their **water content falls to about 10–15 percent** by mass; general metabolism slows and the embryo may enter **dormancy**. Under favourable conditions (moisture, oxygen, suitable temperature) seeds **germinate**.

sections.heading: 4. Fruits, their significance and dispersal
sections.body_md:
**Fruit.** The ovary develops into the fruit; the ovary wall becomes the **pericarp**, which may be **fleshy** (guava, orange, mango) or **dry** (groundnut, mustard).

- **True fruits** develop only from the **ovary** (mango, coconut, tomato, pea).
- **False fruits** develop from the ovary together with other floral parts, especially the **thalamus** (**apple, strawberry, cashew**).
- **Parthenocarpic fruits** develop **without fertilisation** and are seedless (banana).

**Mango (drupe).** Develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and is one-seeded. Pericarp: thin **epicarp** (skin), fleshy edible **mesocarp**, hard stony **endocarp**, enclosing the seed.

**Coconut (drupe).** Pericarp: smooth **epicarp**, thick **fibrous mesocarp** (coir), hard **endocarp** (shell). The seed has a **white solid endosperm** (kernel) and **liquid endosperm** (coconut water), and a small embryo below one of the three “eyes”. The fibrous mesocarp makes the fruit buoyant, aiding dispersal by water.

**Significance of seeds and fruits:**
- Pollination and fertilisation are **independent of water**, and seed formation is more dependable.
- Seeds have food reserves for the young seedling until it can photosynthesise.
- A hard seed coat protects the embryo; **dormancy** and long viability allow storage — a **lupine** seed (Lupinus arcticus) about **10,000 years** old and a **date palm** (Phoenix dactylifera) seed about **2,000 years** old have germinated.
- As products of sexual reproduction, seeds generate **new genetic combinations** (variation).
- Seeds are the basis of agriculture; fruits **protect** seeds and help their **dispersal**.
- **Dispersal** (by wind, water and animals) lets plants **colonise new areas** and reduces **crowding and competition** near the parent.

sections.heading: 5. Apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy
sections.body_md:
**Apomixis** is the formation of **seeds without fertilisation**, a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction (found in some species of **Asteraceae** and **grasses**). Ways in which it occurs:
- A **diploid egg cell** forms without reduction division and develops into the embryo without fertilisation.
- Some **nucellar cells** surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

**Importance:** many crop varieties are **hybrids**; if farmers sow seeds collected from a hybrid, the progeny **segregate** and lose the hybrid characters, so new hybrid seed must be bought every year. If hybrids are made **apomictic**, there is **no segregation**, and farmers can keep using the seed. Scientists are trying to identify the genes for apomixis and transfer them into hybrid varieties.

**Polyembryony** is the occurrence of **more than one embryo** in a seed; in **citrus** and **mango**, nucellar cells grow into the embryo sac and form additional embryos.

**Parthenocarpy** is the development of a **fruit without fertilisation**; such fruits are **seedless** (banana). It can be **induced by growth hormones**, and such fruits are commercially valuable.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the endosperm as diploid (it is triploid; perisperm is diploid).
- Calling perisperm "persistent endosperm" (it is persistent nucellus).
- Saying the coleoptile covers the radicle (it covers the plumule; the coleorhiza covers the radicle).
- Calling apple a true fruit (the thalamus forms most of it).
- Saying we eat the mesocarp of coconut (we eat the endosperm).
- Confusing apomixis (seed without fertilisation) with parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilisation).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: ploidy, examples, a reason, an analogy, a term.
- 2–3-mark questions: double fertilisation and its significance; endosperm types; seed and fruit diagrams; differences between pairs.
- 5-mark questions in parts: double fertilisation with diagram and ploidy; embryo development; seed structures; apomixis and its use in agriculture.
- Diagrams: L.S. of maize grain, bean seed, mango and coconut, dicot and monocot embryos, drawn in pencil and labelled.

questions.stem_md: What is double fertilisation? State its significance.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the events from the entry of the pollen tube into the ovule to the formation of the zygote and the primary endosperm nucleus. [3]
(b) A plant has 2n = 18. State the number of chromosomes in (i) the zygote, (ii) the endosperm, (iii) a cell of the seed coat, and (iv) an antipodal cell before it degenerates. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The pollen tube enters the ovule through the **micropyle** and then enters one of the **synergids**, guided by the **filiform apparatus**. It discharges **two male gametes** into the synergid's cytoplasm. One male gamete moves to the **egg cell** and fuses with its nucleus (**syngamy**), forming the **diploid zygote**. The other moves to the **central cell** and fuses with the **two polar nuclei** (**triple fusion**), forming the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus**; the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell. These two fusions make up **double fertilisation**.

(b) With $n = 9$: (i) zygote **18**; (ii) endosperm **27**; (iii) seed coat **18** (maternal, from the integuments); (iv) antipodal **9** (haploid).

questions.stem_md: Describe the three types of endosperm development, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nuclear:** the primary endosperm nucleus divides repeatedly by **free-nuclear** division; walls may form later from the periphery — e.g. **coconut**, whose water is free-nuclear and kernel cellular.
2. **Cellular:** every nuclear division is followed by **wall formation** — e.g. **Petunia, Datura**.
3. **Helobial:** the first division gives **two unequal cells**; the larger divides free-nuclearly and the smaller cellularly or not at all — common in **monocots**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between albuminous and non-albuminous seeds, giving two examples of each.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State three advantages that seeds have given to flowering plants. [3]
(b) Seeds of an arctic lupine about 10,000 years old germinated. What does this show about seeds, and why is this property important to agriculture? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. Pollination and fertilisation do **not depend on water**, so seed formation is more dependable. 2. Seeds carry **food reserves** that nourish the young seedling until it can photosynthesise, and a **hard seed coat** protects the embryo. 3. Being products of sexual reproduction, seeds produce **new genetic combinations** (variation); with fruits they also allow **dispersal** to new habitats.

(b) It shows that seeds can remain **dormant** and **viable** for very long periods because of their low water content and slowed metabolism. This matters to agriculture because seeds can be **stored** as food and as **planting material** for later seasons.

questions.stem_md: What is apomixis? Describe two ways in which it can occur, and explain its importance in hybrid seed production.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Apomixis** is the formation of **seeds without fertilisation**, found in some Asteraceae and grasses. It can occur when (i) a **diploid egg** forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation, or (ii) **nucellar cells** around the embryo sac divide, protrude into it and develop into embryos.

**Importance:** seeds of hybrids **segregate**, so farmers must buy new hybrid seed every year; **apomictic hybrids** would not segregate, so seed could be **reused**.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two ways; importance.

questions.stem_md: A fruit grower notices (i) seedless fruits on one variety, (ii) several seedlings from a single seed of another, and (iii) seeds formed on plants whose flowers were bagged and never pollinated. Name the phenomenon in each case and give one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Parthenocarpy** — development of a fruit without fertilisation, so the fruit is seedless, e.g. **banana**.

(ii) **Polyembryony** — more than one embryo in a seed, often because nucellar cells grow into extra embryos, e.g. **citrus** or **mango**.

(iii) **Apomixis** — seed formation without fertilisation, since the bagged flowers received no pollen, e.g. some **Asteraceae** and **grasses**.

questions.solution_md: Three phenomena with examples.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between apomixis and parthenocarpy. [2]
(b) A seed company sells hybrid maize seed. Farmers who saved and sowed seed from their hybrid crop got uneven plants with lower yields. Explain why, and how apomixis could solve the problem. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Apomixis** is the formation of **seeds** without fertilisation (the embryo forms from a diploid egg or from nucellar cells), e.g. some Asteraceae and grasses. **Parthenocarpy** is the formation of **fruits** without fertilisation; such fruits are **seedless**, e.g. banana.

(b) A hybrid is **heterozygous** for many genes. When its seeds are formed by sexual reproduction, the genes **segregate**, so the next generation is a mixture of genotypes; plants are uneven and many lose the hybrid vigour and yield. If the hybrid were **apomictic**, its seeds would form **without fertilisation** and be **genetically identical** to the hybrid parent, so there would be **no segregation** and farmers could **reuse the seed** every year.

questions.solution_md: Distinction; segregation; apomixis as solution.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Apomictic seed identical to parent; reuse
